content: In August 2016, a stakeholder meeting of the Implementing Best Practices (IBP) Consortium was convened in Washington, DC. The purpose of this meeting was to gather input and insights from implementation experts and partners. Following this, revisions to the draft implementation guide were reviewed with the original working group members during a teleconference in November 2016. A second in-person meeting with the working group, including IBP members, was held in March 2017. During these meetings, participants discussed the definitions of adoption and adaptation in the context of developing the implementation guide for the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) and Selected Practice Recommendations (SPR). The term adoption, in the context of local use of international guidelines, has not been formally defined. However, it is informally used to describe the direct incorporation of WHO-published tools, such as the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria Wheel for contraceptive use (referred to as the MEC wheel), into local clinical settings. According to the WHO document Introducing WHO’s reproductive health guidelines and tools into national programmes: principles and processes of adaptation and implementation, adaptation involves transforming an externally developed guideline or tool into an accepted product that fits a particular country’s or region’s needs, circumstances, and context. This process may include updating or revising existing national guidelines and tools. The MEC also addresses adaptation, stating that the guidance in the document is intended to be interpreted at the country and program levels in a way that reflects the diversity of situations and settings in which contraceptives are provided. While the classification of categories in the document is unlikely to change during this process, the application of these categories at the country level will likely vary. For example, the MEC wheel may be used without modifications. Therefore, in this document, the term adaptation is defined as a process to incorporate the most updated WHO MEC and SPR guidance into national family planning guidelines and to implement these evidence-based guidelines in practice. The implementation process is divided into several stages, each with specific goals and activities: 1. Exploration Stage: This stage involves mapping the current country family planning guidelines and assessing their use. The goal is to evaluate the country’s need and readiness for implementing the MEC and SPR guidance. Activities include identifying key stakeholders, resources, and personnel, as well as conducting a readiness assessment to determine the next steps for implementation. 2. Installation Stage: Practical preparations are made to initiate revisions to the national family planning guidelines based on the MEC/SPR guidance. This includes securing resources, developing adapted guidelines, and conducting capacity-building activities. Communication protocols are established, and financial and human resources are secured. Training and support are provided to those expected to implement the guidelines. 3. Initial Implementation Stage: During this stage, the revised national family planning guidelines are rolled out. Existing processes within a setting must be altered, leading to changes in organizational roles, functions, and structures. Updated family planning guidelines and materials are put to use, and intensive coaching of practitioners by local implementation team members is critical. Problems may arise, requiring the team to develop strategies for continuous improvement and rapid-cycle problem-solving. Metrics from monitoring and evaluation are used to assess implementation quality, identify problems, and inform decision-making. 4. Full Implementation Stage: This stage occurs once the new family planning guidelines are fully integrated into organizational and provider practices, policies, and procedures. The goal is for the new guidelines to become standard practice. Monitoring and evaluation continue at the local level as more staff members participate and turnover occurs. Full implementation of a change is challenging to achieve and sustain without necessary implementation supports. Throughout all stages, programmatic sustainability must be considered. This involves providing ongoing training, coaching, monitoring, and evaluation to ensure the guidelines remain effective and relevant. Mechanisms should be developed to periodically review and revise national guidelines and tools to align with ongoing updates to the MEC and SPR. To support the implementation process, a national implementation team should be established under the leadership of the Ministry of Health (MOH). This team should include key stakeholders in reproductive health and family planning service delivery, such as representatives from the public health department, WHO country office, medical training institutions, partner NGOs, faith-based organizations, private sector healthcare providers, and community health workers. Stakeholder meetings should be conducted to explore and begin integrating the MEC/SPR guidance. These meetings should include activities such as briefing stakeholders on the basis for integration, determining the country’s commitment and capacity for incorporating the guidance, setting clear goals, and initiating a needs assessment to identify gaps and inconsistencies in national guidelines compared to WHO guidance. A communication plan should be developed to describe the implementation objectives and processes. Effective communication routes among policymakers, program managers, and front-line health workers should be identified and established. Local implementation teams should be formed to take responsibility for local changes. Finally, mechanisms should be created to continually assess and improve family planning service delivery. This includes developing a monitoring and evaluation program for adherence to the MEC/SPR guidance, incorporating principles of rapid-cycle problem-solving, and ensuring that any updates to the MEC/SPR guidance are disseminated and incorporated into national guidelines, policies, and standards.
